units.t: Food & Cooking Shorts. Episode three.

In this episode: Escoffier: the chef who organised the kitchen, Pavlova, lamingtons and pies: Australia's food icons, Sugar: a sweet substance with a bitter past and The spice trade: flavours that built empires.
Part one. Escoffier: the chef who organised the kitchen.
Every time a cook answers ‘Yes, chef’, they echo one man.
Auguste Escoffier turned chaotic kitchens into disciplined teams, and named a dessert after an Australian soprano.
Order from chaos.
Georges Auguste Escoffier was born in 1846 in Villeneuve-Loubet, near Nice.
At around thirteen he began an apprenticeship in his uncle's restaurant, then worked his way up through Paris kitchens.
During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 he cooked for the French army, an experience of feeding large numbers under pressure that many writers think shaped his ideas about organisation.
Kitchens of the time were brutal.
Coal-fired ranges made them extremely hot, ventilation was poor and cooks often drank heavily through long shifts.
One cook might spend hours making a whole dish while another did nearly the same beside him.
Service à la russe, with courses brought out one after another, was replacing service à la française, with many dishes placed on the table together, and it demanded tighter timing.
The brigade system.
Escoffier's lasting innovation was the brigade de cuisine, a kitchen run like a well-drilled team.
At the top sits the chef de cuisine, with a sous chef second in command.

Each station is led by a chef de partie: the saucier handles sauces and sautéed dishes, the rôtisseur roasts, the poissonnier cooks fish, the entremetier handles vegetables and soups, the garde manger prepares cold foods and the pâtissier makes pastry and desserts.
Junior cooks, called commis, work under each leader.
Because stations prepare components in parallel, a complex dish can be assembled in minutes rather than hours.
He also pushed for calmer behaviour, discouraging shouting, drinking and smoking on duty, and insisting on clean uniforms.
The structure and its French titles are still used worldwide, including in Australia.
Ritz and the Savoy.
In Monte Carlo, Escoffier met the Swiss hotelier César Ritz, and the two formed one of history's great hospitality partnerships.
In 1890 they took charge of London's new Savoy Hotel, where Escoffier's cooking drew royalty, aristocrats and celebrities.
They helped make dining in an elegant hotel restaurant fashionable, including for well-to-do women, who had been less likely to dine in public.
The Savoy partnership ended in 1898, when Ritz and Escoffier were dismissed amid a dispute with the owners over alleged financial irregularities.
They moved on quickly.
Ritz opened his famous Paris hotel that year, with Escoffier running the kitchen, and the pair then opened the Carlton Hotel in London, where Escoffier cooked for many years.
Peach Melba.
Escoffier liked to name dishes after famous guests, and his best-known tribute was to an Australian.
Nellie Melba, born Helen Porter Mitchell in Melbourne, took her stage name from her home city and became one of the most celebrated sopranos of her time.
While she performed in London in the 1890s, Escoffier created a dessert in her honour: poached peaches served on vanilla ice cream.
An early presentation was reportedly served in a swan carved from ice, a nod to the opera Lohengrin.
Raspberry sauce joined the classic recipe a few years later.
Melba toast, crisp thin slices of dry toast, is also traditionally linked to the singer and Escoffier's kitchens.
The guide and the legacy.
In 1903 Escoffier published Le Guide Culinaire, written with colleagues, which gathered thousands of recipes into a single reference still read by chefs.
Marie-Antoine Carême had earlier grouped French sauces.
Escoffier's system is usually summarised as five mother sauces: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, hollandaise and tomato.
Learn these and you can make hundreds of variations.
He also championed simplicity over towering decoration, his motto often given as "faites simple", focused on flavour rather than display.
He supported charities for retired cooks and worked to make cooking respected as a skilled career.
He was later made a knight of the Legion of Honour and died in 1935, aged 88.
His influence lives on in stations, titles and the call-and-response of "Yes, chef", and in the idea that a kitchen should run calmly, cleanly and on time.
The key idea: Before Escoffier, grand kitchens were hot, disorganised places where cooks duplicated work.
Part two. Pavlova, lamingtons and pies: Australia's food icons.
Who really invented the pavlova?
Why can't you sell an ‘Anzac cookie’?
The stories behind Australia's favourite foods are full of rivalries, legends and law.
Contested origins.
The pavlova is named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, who toured Australia and New Zealand in 1926 and 1929.
Australians long credited Bert Sachse of Perth's Esplanade Hotel with creating it in 1935.
But the New Zealand food historian Helen Leach found New Zealand recipes called pavlova from the late 1920s.
She also found similar meringue cakes in Europe and the United States long before either country named one after a dancer.
The friendly argument is unlikely ever to end.
The lamington is a sponge square dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut.
It is named after Lord Lamington, Governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901.
The popular story credits his French-born chef, Armand Galland, with inventing it to use up stale sponge, but historians cannot confirm it.
Anzac biscuits and the law.
Anzac biscuits are made from rolled oats, flour, sugar, butter, golden syrup and usually desiccated coconut, with no eggs.
They are linked to the First World War, but historians think oat biscuits were mainly baked and sold at home to raise money for the war effort, not standard soldiers' food.
Troops were issued a notoriously hard ration biscuit, jokingly called an Anzac tile or wafer.
The name Anzac itself is protected under Australian law, and using it commercially needs approval from the Minister for Veterans' Affairs.
Products may be sold as Anzac biscuits if they stick to the traditional recipe and shape.
Calling them ‘Anzac cookies’ is not normally allowed, because of the American association.
The meat pie.
Australians are devoted to the meat pie: minced or chunky beef in gravy inside a pastry case, eaten by hand at football games, bakeries and service stations.
The tradition came from Britain, but Australians made it their own, with brands, bakery competitions and fierce local loyalties.
Variations abound, including curry pies, steak and kidney, and the pie with tomato sauce on top.
Adelaide is famous for the pie floater, a meat pie served upside down in a bowl of thick green pea soup, often topped with tomato sauce and once sold from late-night pie carts.
Debates about the right pastry, gravy and filling still run hot, and many bakeries now offer gourmet and vegetarian versions.
Borrowed and reinvented.
In 1951 the Bendigo boilermaker Frank McEncroe launched the Chiko Roll at the Wagga Wagga Agricultural Show.
Inspired by Chinese spring rolls, it wrapped cabbage, celery, barley, carrot, beef and seasonings in thick, deep-fried pastry, tough enough to eat on the move.
The Australian dim sim, loosely based on Cantonese dumplings such as siu mai, is usually credited to Melbourne's Wing Lee restaurant in the 1940s.
It is larger and meatier, steamed or deep fried, and often eaten with soy sauce.
In the 1950s, Arnott's food technologist Ian Norris came across Britain's Penguin biscuit overseas.
In 1964 Arnott's launched the Tim Tam, named after the racehorse that won the 1958 Kentucky Derby.
Fans invented the ‘Tim Tam slam’, using the biscuit as a straw for hot drinks.
Becoming an icon.
Look closely at almost any national dish and you find borrowing.

Meat pies came from Britain, pavlova from a long European meringue tradition, the Chiko Roll and dim sim from Chinese cooking, and the flat white from a cafe culture shaped by Italian and other migrants.
Long before any of this, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples ate a rich range of native foods, an older story still.
Origin tales tend to be colourful and hard to verify: a chef inventing a cake for unexpected guests, a dessert created in one inspired moment.
Historians who dig into old cookbooks and newspapers often find gradual change rather than one inventor.
What makes a food iconic is less its birth than the memories, rituals and pride people build around it.
The key idea: Pavlova and lamingtons are Australian icons whose true origins are disputed or unknown.
Part three. Sugar: a sweet substance with a bitter past.
Sugar began as a rare spice and a medicine.
Its rise to everyday sweetness was driven by slavery, wars and, in Queensland, a painful chapter of Australian history.
From reed to luxury.
Sugarcane is a giant grass first domesticated in New Guinea thousands of years ago.
People chewed the stalks for their sweet juice.
In India, they learned to boil the juice down into crystals, at least by the early centuries AD.
The word sugar descends from the Sanskrit sharkara, and candy from khanda.
Greek writers who met Alexander the Great's forces in India described a reed that made honey without bees.
Arab and Persian cultivators spread cane and refining across the Mediterranean, and to medieval Europeans sugar was a luxury used in medicine and feasts.
That changed when Europeans grew cane on Atlantic islands such as Madeira, then in the Americas: Columbus took it to Hispaniola in 1493.
Prices fell and demand soared, and in Britain sweetened tea became part of daily life.
Slavery and the boycott.
Sugar was hard, dangerous work.
Cane had to be crushed and boiled quickly after cutting, so mills and boiling houses ran around the clock.
Brazil and then Caribbean islands such as Barbados and Jamaica became huge producers, and owners met their labour demand through the transatlantic slave trade.
Millions of enslaved Africans were shipped to the Americas, many to sugar colonies where death rates were terrible.
Historians see sugar as a central engine of the slave economy.
In the early 1790s, British pamphlets urged families to stop buying slave-grown sugar, and around 300,000 people took part.
Women, who largely controlled household shopping but could not vote, were central.
Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most colonies from 1834.
The boycott is an early example of ethical consumption.
Napoleon and the beet.
In 1747 the German chemist Andreas Marggraf showed that sugar crystals from beets were identical to cane sugar.
His student Franz Achard bred beets with more sugar and opened the first beet sugar factory in Silesia in 1801.
War made the difference.
During the Napoleonic Wars, the British naval blockade cut France off from Caribbean cane sugar.
Napoleon backed beet sugar with land grants, funding and decrees in the early 1810s, and factories sprang up.
The industry survived the war, and a significant share of the world's sugar now comes from beets grown in cooler climates.
Chemically, white sugar from cane and from beet is the same molecule: sucrose.
Queensland and blackbirding.
Sugar became a major Queensland industry from the 1860s.

Planters wanted cheap labour for hot, punishing work, and between 1863 and 1904 around 60,000 people from Pacific islands, especially today's Vanuatu and Solomon Islands, were brought to Queensland under labour contracts.
Some came willingly, but many were tricked, coerced or kidnapped, a practice known as blackbirding.
Wages were low, conditions harsh and death rates high.
After Federation, the Pacific Island Labourers Act of 1901 led to the deportation of most Islanders, as part of the White Australia policy.
Some stayed, and their descendants form the Australian South Sea Islander community, formally recognised by the Commonwealth in 1994.
The cane toad was also introduced in 1935 to fight cane beetles.
Sugar and your body.
Table sugar, sucrose, is one glucose and one fructose unit joined together, and your gut quickly splits it apart.
Honey, maple syrup, coconut sugar and raw sugar are mostly the same simple sugars in slightly different proportions, with only trace amounts of anything else, so they are not much healthier.
The World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of daily energy, and suggests below 5 percent brings further benefits.
Free sugars are those added to food, plus those in honey, syrups and juices.
Sugars naturally inside whole fruit, milk and vegetables are not counted.
Sugary drinks are the biggest single source for many people, and they are strongly linked to tooth decay and weight gain.
The key idea: Sugarcane, first domesticated in New Guinea, became a rare spice and medicine before Europe's supplies grew and it turned into an everyday staple.
Part four. The spice trade: flavours that built empires.
Pepper, cloves and nutmeg were once worth fighting and dying for.
The hunt for spices sent ships around the world, made fortunes and caused terrible violence.
Rare, far and precious.
A jar of nutmeg costs a few dollars today, but spices were once luxuries because they grew in so few places.
Black pepper came from Kerala's Malabar Coast, true cinnamon from Sri Lanka, cloves from a handful of northern Moluccan islands, and nutmeg and mace almost entirely from the tiny Banda Islands.
Indian, Arab, Malay, Chinese and other merchants carried them, each adding a markup.
The trade is ancient.
Romans loved pepper, and merchants used the monsoon winds to cross from Egypt's Red Sea ports to India in weeks.
According to ancient accounts, Alaric demanded thousands of pounds of pepper when he besieged Rome in 408.
A popular belief says spices hid the taste of rotting meat.
Most historians reject it: spices often cost far more than fresh meat.
Race for a sea route.
In the medieval period, spices reached Europe through Middle Eastern routes and Italian cities such as Venice, which grew rich as middlemen.
Other European powers wanted to cut them out.
Portugal pushed down the coast of Africa, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama rounded the Cape of Good Hope and reached Calicut in India by sea.
Spain sponsored Christopher Columbus, who sailed west in 1492 hoping to reach Asia.
He reached the Caribbean instead, where he met chillies and allspice.
He called the chillies 'peppers', a name that has confused people ever since.
Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, which completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1522, was also largely a search for a route to the spice islands.
Monopolies and massacres.
In the seventeenth century the Dutch East India Company, the VOC, set out to control the most valuable spices completely.
Its methods were brutal.
In 1621 forces under governor-general Jan Pieterszoon Coen conquered the Banda Islands, the world's only real source of nutmeg.
Most Bandanese were killed, enslaved or driven away, and the islands became plantations worked by enslaved people.
The Dutch also restricted clove trees to particular islands and destroyed trees elsewhere to keep prices high.
When England and the Netherlands made peace in 1667, the Dutch kept Run, a tiny nutmeg island the English had held, while England kept New Amsterdam, which it had seized and renamed New York.
In hindsight, the deal looks rather different.
How spices got cheap.
Monopolies over living plants rarely last.
In the 1770s a French official, Pierre Poivre, organised expeditions that smuggled clove and nutmeg seedlings out of the Dutch-controlled islands to Mauritius and other French colonies.
During the Napoleonic Wars the British also moved spice plants to places such as Ceylon and Penang, and nutmeg later reached Grenada, which still has one on its flag.
Clove growing became a major industry on Zanzibar, worked by enslaved people.
As spices were grown in more places, prices fell.
European tastes also shifted towards sugar, coffee, tea and chocolate.
Spices once worth a fortune became ordinary kitchen staples, sold cheaply in jars all over the world.
Saffron, vanilla and legacy.
Some spices stay expensive because they take so much work.
Saffron, usually the priciest by weight, is the thread-like stigmas of a crocus.
Each flower has only three, picked by hand, so a kilogram needs well over a hundred thousand flowers.
Iran grows most of it, with small amounts from Tasmania.
Vanilla is the cured pod of a Mexican orchid.
Elsewhere its natural pollinators are missing, until in 1841 Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy on Reunion, devised the quick hand-pollination method still used today.
The trade moved plants, people and ideas.
Chillies became central to Indian, Thai, Sichuan and Korean food, and pepper sits beside salt on most Western tables.
It also left a legacy of conquest, monopoly, slavery and environmental change.
The key idea: For most of history spices were luxuries because they grew in few places and passed through many hands.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What problem did Escoffier face in nineteenth century kitchens?
Answer. Hot, chaotic kitchens with duplicated work.
Question two. What does the evidence suggest about the pavlova's origin?
Answer. Earlier recipes exist in New Zealand and Europe.
Question three. Why did sugar change from a rare luxury to an everyday staple in Europe?
Answer. More cane grown in the Americas lowered prices.
Question four. Why do most historians reject the idea that spices hid the taste of rotten meat?
Answer. Spices often cost far more than fresh meat.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
